_comment: The English catalogue. Every string is transcribed from the approved click dummy, which owns the words as well as the layout, EXCEPT the pending.* block - that declares an unbuilt screen and is new app-side copy. GATE 4 was granted on 2026-09-05 and the 38 approved changes are in the dummy; the ones that touch a screen this app has built are reflected here. A change is written into the dummy first and copied here second, never the other way round.
app.name: windowsweep
nav.label: Main
theme.title: Appearance
home.heroSubUnmeasured: Nothing has been measured yet. A scan reads sizes and deletes nothing.
home.developerOff: Off. Toolchain caches are left alone.
home.developerNote: The idle gate keeps anything you have used in the last hundred days, which is the point: the next install should still be fast.
home.assure: Your documents, photos, keys and saved passwords are never touched - not by a flag, not by a profile, not by accident, whatever you click here.
run.dryRunNote: This was a dry-run. Run the same thing without it to reclaim the space.
sections.title: Sections
sections.lede: The catalogue is a frozen public contract - a number is never reused, and a retired section becomes a no-op that says so.
consent.title: Nothing leaves this machine unless you turn it on.
consent.lede: The cleanup engine makes zero network calls - its own test suite asserts that, and it is true whether you accept anything below or not. What follows is only about the desktop window you are looking at.
consent.provider.ga4.name: Product analytics
consent.provider.ga4.what: Which screens you opened and which buttons you pressed.
consent.provider.amplitude.name: Behaviour analytics
consent.provider.amplitude.what: The same events, sent to a second destination so a funnel can be read across releases.
consent.provider.clarity.name: Session replay
consent.provider.clarity.what: A recording of this window with every piece of text masked.
consent.provider.sentry.name: Crash reports
consent.provider.sentry.what: A stack trace when something breaks, with file paths stripped out.
consent.detailsSummary: What each one would receive, in plain terms
consent.neverSentLabel: Never sent, by any of them:
consent.neverSent: a file path, a folder name, a drive label, your user name, your machine name, or the contents of anything. A run summary is a count and a number of bytes.
consent.eachOne: Each is individually revocable later, in Settings, and revoking one stops it immediately.
consent.decliningIsFine: Declining is a first-class answer. The app is not degraded, nothing asks you again, and every feature including sign-in and sync still works.
consent.summaryNone: Nothing is switched on. The app works exactly the same.
consent.summaryAll: All four are on. You can revoke any of them in Settings, and it stops immediately.
consent.summarySome: {{count}} of {{total}} are on. The rest stay off until you say otherwise.
pending.title: This screen is specified and not yet translated.
pending.body: The click dummy specifies it in full and this window does not carry it yet. It is named here rather than hidden, so what is missing is a stated gap rather than something you have to discover.
pending.reference: Specified in the click dummy at
common.loading: Reading the catalogue from the engine
error.engineMissing: The cleanup engine did not start. Reinstall windowsweep, or run the command-line tool once to confirm it works.
splash.detailsSummary: What happens while this is on screen
splash.detailsWhat: Three things, none of which touch your disk: the bundled engine reports its version, the catalogue is read from `--list --json` so a new section appears without an app update, and the updater checks whether a newer build exists.
splash.detailsNothing: Nothing is scanned and nothing is deleted until you ask. If the update check cannot reach the network it is skipped silently - reclaiming space has never needed it.
settings.title: Settings
settings.lede: Every one of these maps to a flag the engine already has, so anything you set here you can also pass on a command line.
settings.noKeys: No destination is configured in this build, so nothing could be sent even with a switch on.
settings.about: windowsweep reclaims disk space on Windows. It names every path before it touches one, and refuses your documents, credentials and browser state outright. The desktop window drives the same engine the command-line tool runs.
history.title: History
history.emptyTitle: windowsweep has not run on this machine yet.
history.emptyBody: A dry-run costs nothing and deletes nothing.
history.signedOutNote: Signed out, so this is this machine only. Signing in brings the runs from your other machines alongside these.
picker.title: Nothing here goes unless you choose it.
picker.lede: A safe run never touches these. The engine offered every row below; the ones you tick are the ones that go, and the rest are left exactly as they are.
picker.emptyBody: The sections that ask a person to choose - stale project artefacts, partial downloads, large idle files in Downloads, orphaned application data - populate this screen when one of them runs.
picker.consequence: The Recycle Bin can be emptied later. Permanent has no undo.
report.emptyBody: A report is written for every run, including a dry-run, and the file on disk says exactly what this screen says.
report.onDisk: The same report, on disk at
account.title: Sign in only if you want your settings on another machine.
account.lede: Reclaiming space is never gated. Signing in moves your settings and a summary of each run between your own machines, and that is all it does.
account.whatSyncs: What syncs, per run: the date, the mode, whether it was a dry-run, whether it was elevated, which section numbers ran, the bytes reclaimed, the bytes a dry-run estimated, how long it took, and an id. Plus your appearance settings, developer mode, and a last-seen timestamp.
account.whatNeverSyncs: What never syncs: a file path, a folder name, a drive label, your machine name or your Windows user name.
account.signOutNote: Signing out clears every local trace of the account, including the rows cached from your other machines.
account.notConfigured: Sign-in is not configured in this build
account.notConfiguredNote: The OAuth client id is absent, so this build cannot sign in. Everything else works exactly the same.
elevation.title: {{count}} sections need Windows to ask your permission.
elevation.lede: windowsweep never elevates itself. When you ask for one of these, it opens a second, elevated window that does that work and writes its own report. This window keeps running, unelevated, and shows you the log as it arrives.
elevation.whatHappens: What happens when you press it
elevation.step.asks.title: Windows asks you.
elevation.step.asks.body: The standard User Account Control prompt, from Windows, not from windowsweep. If you say no, nothing happens and nothing is written.
elevation.step.second.title: A second window opens.
elevation.step.second.body: It runs only the sections you chose, with --reports-dir and --logs-dir pointed at this run’s folder.
elevation.step.tails.title: This window tails the log.
elevation.step.tails.body: You watch it from here. The elevated window closes itself when it is done, and its exit code comes back to this one.
elevation.step.reports.title: Both reports land side by side.
elevation.measureNote: A scan can measure these sections without administrator rights. It cannot clear them.
elevation.smartScreenSummary: Windows may warn you the first time you install this
elevation.smartScreenWhy: The installer is not signed with a paid code-signing certificate, so Microsoft SmartScreen shows “Windows protected your PC” on first run. That is a statement about the certificate, not about the file.
elevation.smartScreenHow: Choose More info and then Run anyway. You can verify what you downloaded first: every release publishes a SHA-256 checksum for each installer, and a minisign signature the app’s own updater checks. Neither is a code-signing certificate - they prove the file is the one that was built, not who built it. The source is public.
elevation.smartScreenWhyHere: This note is here rather than hidden because meeting that dialog unexplained is worse than reading about it in advance.
